container image.summary: A container image is an immutable layered filesystem + config/metadata used to create containers.
container image.problem: It packages an app with its runtime dependencies so it runs consistently across environments.
container image.mechanics: Build produces layered tars hashed by content; run instantiates a writable container layer on top. Pull fetches by name:tag or digest from a registry.
container image.tradeoffs: Fat images slow deploys and widen CVE surface; distroless/minimal images trade debug ease for security. Pin digests for reproducibility.
container image.troubleshoot: Unexpected versions: you pulled :latest. Scan and pin digests. Debug with docker history and dive.
container image.example:
docker build -t api:1.2 .
docker image ls
docker pull ghcr.io/org/api@sha256:…
container image.integration: 1) Define a standard base image. 2) Build in CI and push digests. 3) Scan on push. 4) Deploy by digest.

Dockerfile layer.summary: Dockerfile layers cache filesystem diffs from each instruction; ordering affects build-cache hit rates.
Dockerfile layer.problem: Good layering makes rebuilds fast when only app code changes.
Dockerfile layer.mechanics: Docker executes instructions sequentially, reusing cached layers until an input changes. Put dependency install before COPY of source so code edits don't reinstall deps.
Dockerfile layer.tradeoffs: Over-splitting layers can hurt pull size less than you'd think (squash exists elsewhere); clarity + cache locality matter most.
Dockerfile layer.troubleshoot: Cache never hits: check changing ARG/COPY order and build context noise—use .dockerignore.
Dockerfile layer.example:
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build
Dockerfile layer.integration: 1) Order Dockerfile for cache. 2) Add .dockerignore. 3) Use BuildKit cache in CI. 4) Measure build times.

multi-stage build.summary: Multi-stage Docker builds compile in a fat builder stage and copy artifacts into a slim runtime stage.
multi-stage build.problem: It keeps final images small without shipping compilers/dev deps.
multi-stage build.mechanics: First stage installs toolchains and builds; final stage starts FROM a minimal image and COPY --from=builder the binary/assets only.
multi-stage build.tradeoffs: More stages add complexity; worthwhile when build tools dwarf runtime. Ensure glibc/musl compatibility for binaries.
multi-stage build.troubleshoot: Missing files in final image: wrong COPY path/stage name. Debug by running the builder stage interactively.
multi-stage build.example:
FROM golang:1.22 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/api
FROM gcr.io/distroless/static
COPY --from=build /out/api /api
ENTRYPOINT ["/api"]
multi-stage build.integration: 1) Split build vs runtime. 2) Copy only artifacts. 3) Scan final image. 4) Pin both bases by digest.

Docker Compose service.summary: A Compose service defines a containerized dependency (build/image, ports, env, networks, volumes) for local/dev stacks.
Docker Compose service.problem: It runs multi-container apps with one declarative file instead of ad-hoc docker run scripts.
Docker Compose service.mechanics: compose up creates network, starts services, and DNS-resolves service names. depends_on waits for start (not readiness unless healthchecks configured).
Docker Compose service.tradeoffs: Compose is not a production orchestrator—use Swarm/k8s for prod HA. Healthchecks matter for ordering.
Docker Compose service.troubleshoot: Cannot reach db: wrong network, hostname, or published vs internal ports. Use compose logs and exec.
Docker Compose service.example:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    environment: { DATABASE_URL: postgres://db:5432/app }
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    volumes: ["pg:/var/lib/postgresql/data"]
Docker Compose service.integration: 1) Model each process as a service. 2) Use internal DNS names. 3) Add healthchecks. 4) Keep secrets out of compose committed files.

bridge network.summary: A Docker bridge network is a software bridge connecting containers so they can communicate via private IPs and embedded DNS.
bridge network.problem: User-defined bridges provide service-name DNS; the default bridge is more limited.
bridge network.mechanics: Containers on the same user-defined network resolve each other by name. Publishing ports maps host→container for external access.
bridge network.tradeoffs: Host networking skips isolation (Linux) for performance/special cases. Overlay networks span Swarm/k8s nodes differently.
bridge network.troubleshoot: Name resolution fails on default bridge—attach a user-defined network. Port conflicts on host publishes.
bridge network.example:
docker network create appnet
docker run -d --network appnet --name redis redis:7
bridge network.integration: 1) Create explicit networks per app. 2) Avoid legacy links. 3) Publish only needed ports. 4) Document inter-service hostnames.

image registry.summary: An image registry stores and serves container images (Docker Hub, ECR, GHCR, GCR) by repository and tag/digest.
image registry.problem: It is the distribution point between CI builds and runtime pulls.
image registry.mechanics: CI pushes image; clusters pull with credentials. Prefer digest pins in prod manifests. Retention policies garbage-collect old tags.
image registry.tradeoffs: Public registries risk rate limits; private registries add auth/ops. Mutable tags (:latest) undermine provenance.
image registry.troubleshoot: Pull denials: auth, IAM, or network policy. Verify digests match what CI pushed.
image registry.integration: 1) Use a private registry. 2) Push immutable tags+digests. 3) Restrict pull access. 4) Set retention and scanning.

volume.summary: A Docker/k8s volume provides durable or shared filesystem storage that outlives a container’s writable layer.
volume.problem: It persists databases and uploads without baking data into images.
volume.mechanics: Declare a volume and mount at a path; engine manages named volumes, bind mounts map host paths. Data remains after container removal for named volumes.
volume.tradeoffs: Bind mounts are convenient locally but fragile in prod. Backing storage performance/IOPS matter for DBs.
volume.troubleshoot: Permission errors: container user vs volume ownership. Lost data: volume not mounted or wrong name.
volume.example:
docker volume create pgdata
docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16
volume.integration: 1) Use named volumes for stateful local deps. 2) Plan backups. 3) Align UIDs. 4) In k8s use PVCs.

Kubernetes.summary: Kubernetes orchestrates containers by reconciling declared desired state for workloads, networking, and storage across a cluster.
Kubernetes.problem: It standardizes deploy/scale/self-heal so you are not managing pets by SSH.
Kubernetes.mechanics: You apply objects; controllers reconcile actual toward desired. Deployments manage Pods; Services route to Pods; kubelet runs probes.
Kubernetes.tradeoffs: K8s complexity is real—managed control planes help. Not every app needs k8s; Compose/ECS can be enough early.
Kubernetes.troubleshoot: CrashLoopBackOff: kubectl describe/logs. Pending: scheduling/resources/taints. Use events.
Kubernetes.example:
kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml
kubectl get pods -o wide
kubectl rollout status deploy/api
Kubernetes.integration: 1) Start with Deployment+Service. 2) Add probes/resources. 3) GitOps manifests. 4) Enforce RBAC least privilege.

Pod.summary: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes: one or more containers sharing network namespace and volumes.
Pod.problem: It colocates tightly coupled containers (app + sidecar) with a shared IP and storage volumes.
Pod.mechanics: Scheduler places the Pod on a node; kubelet starts containers. Pods are mortal—controllers recreate them. Prefer Deployments over naked Pods.
Pod.tradeoffs: Multi-container Pods couple lifecycle; prefer separate Pods unless sidecar pattern is required.
Pod.troubleshoot: Pending: resources/taints/PVC. ImagePullBackOff: registry auth/tag. Describe the Pod.
Pod.example:
kubectl run api --image=ghcr.io/org/api:1.2 --restart=Never
kubectl describe pod api
Pod.integration: 1) Run apps via Deployment. 2) Set resources. 3) Add readiness/liveness. 4) Label for Services.

Deployment.summary: A Deployment declares a desired replica count and Pod template, owning ReplicaSets for rolling updates.
Deployment.problem: It provides declarative rollouts/rollbacks for stateless workloads.
Deployment.mechanics: Changing the Pod template creates a new ReplicaSet and rolls Pods gradually. kubectl rollout undo reverts to a prior revision.
Deployment.tradeoffs: StatefulSets fit sticky identity/storage. DaemonSets fit per-node agents. Jobs fit finite tasks.
Deployment.troubleshoot: Rollout stuck: readiness failing or progressDeadline. Check rollout status and events.
Deployment.example:
kubectl set image deploy/api api=ghcr.io/org/api:1.3
kubectl rollout undo deploy/api
Deployment.integration: 1) Manage apps with Deployments. 2) Tune rolling parameters. 3) Gate on readiness. 4) Alert on stuck rollouts.

Service.summary: A Kubernetes Service provides a stable virtual IP/DNS name load-balancing to matching Pods via selectors.
Service.problem: Pods are ephemeral; Services give clients a consistent endpoint.
Service.mechanics: Service selects Pods by labels; Endpoints/EndpointSlices track ready Pods. ClusterIP is internal; LoadBalancer provisions external IP in cloud.
Service.tradeoffs: ClusterIP is default for east-west. Exposing everything publicly increases attack surface.
Service.troubleshoot: No endpoints: label mismatch or not Ready. Debug with kubectl get endpoints and describe.
Service.integration: 1) Label Pods consistently. 2) Add Service per app. 3) Use Ingress/Gateway for HTTP. 4) Monitor empty endpoints.

ClusterIP.summary: ClusterIP is the default Service type: a virtual IP reachable only inside the cluster.
ClusterIP.problem: It exposes services safely for internal traffic without a public address.
ClusterIP.mechanics: kube-proxy or dataplane DNAT ClusterIP:port to a ready Pod. DNS name service.namespace.svc.cluster.local resolves to ClusterIP.
ClusterIP.tradeoffs: Need external access? Use Ingress/LoadBalancer/NodePort carefully. Headless Services (None) return Pod IPs for stateful patterns.
ClusterIP.troubleshoot: Timeouts: NetworkPolicy, wrong port, or no ready endpoints.
ClusterIP.example:
kubectl get svc api -o wide
kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox -- wget -qO- http://api
ClusterIP.integration: 1) Default to ClusterIP. 2) Front with Ingress for HTTP. 3) Restrict with NetworkPolicy. 4) Test DNS from a debug Pod.

ConfigMap.summary: A ConfigMap stores non-secret configuration as key/value data injectable as env vars or files.
ConfigMap.problem: It separates config from images so the same artifact runs in multiple environments.
ConfigMap.mechanics: Create ConfigMap; reference in Pod spec. Mounted files update depending on kubelet sync; env vars typically need Pod restart.
ConfigMap.tradeoffs: Secrets belong in Secret/KMS—not ConfigMaps. Huge configs better as files than thousands of env vars.
ConfigMap.troubleshoot: App sees old config: env vars not hot-reloaded—roll Pods. Typo in key names.
ConfigMap.integration: 1) Move env into ConfigMaps. 2) Mount files for complex config. 3) Roll Deployments on change. 4) Keep secrets elsewhere.

secret.summary: A Kubernetes Secret stores sensitive key/values (base64 in etcd by default) for credentials and keys.
secret.problem: It keeps passwords/tokens out of images and ConfigMaps.
secret.mechanics: Create Secret; mount as volume or env. Enable encryption at rest and tight RBAC. Prefer CSI/external managers for strong security.
secret.tradeoffs: Secrets in env can leak via process dumps; file mounts with restricted perms are often better. Still not as strong as vaults alone.
secret.troubleshoot: Pull failures: wrong key or RBAC. Audit who can get secrets.
secret.integration: 1) Enable encryption at rest. 2) Restrict Secret RBAC. 3) Prefer external KMS/SealedSecrets/ESO. 4) Rotate regularly.

readiness probe.summary: A readiness probe tells Kubernetes when a container is ready to receive traffic; failing removes Pod from Service endpoints.
readiness probe.problem: It prevents routing to Pods still starting or overloaded.
readiness probe.mechanics: kubelet probes periodically; on failure, Endpoints controller drops the Pod from Services until success returns.
readiness probe.tradeoffs: Liveness restarts; readiness only cuts traffic. Misusing liveness for readiness causes restart storms.
readiness probe.troubleshoot: Flapping readiness: check dependencies and timeouts. Align probe path with real health.
readiness probe.integration: 1) Implement /readyz checking critical deps. 2) Configure readiness on Deployments. 3) Keep liveness separate. 4) Alert on not-ready replicas.

resource request.summary: A CPU/memory request is the guaranteed amount used by the scheduler for placement decisions.
resource request.problem: It enables predictable packing and avoids scheduling onto nodes that cannot meet guarantees.
resource request.mechanics: Scheduler sums requests to find a fit. Burstable QoS occurs when requests < limits. Set requests from measured usage.
resource request.tradeoffs: Requests too high waste capacity; too low cause noisy-neighbor contention. HPA often scales on utilization vs requests.
resource request.troubleshoot: Pending Pods: cluster lacks enough allocatable resources—scale nodes or shrink requests.
resource request.integration: 1) Measure p95 usage. 2) Set requests near steady-state. 3) Set memory limits carefully. 4) Review pending pods.

resource limits.summary: Limits cap the maximum CPU/memory a container may use; memory beyond limit OOMs the container.
resource limits.problem: They protect nodes from a single runaway Pod.
resource limits.mechanics: cgroups enforce limits. CPU limit throttles; memory limit kills on exceed. Prefer accurate requests; limits especially for memory.
resource limits.tradeoffs: Tight CPU limits create latency via throttling. Unbounded memory risks node instability.
resource limits.troubleshoot: OOMKilled: raise memory or fix leak. Throttling: kubectl top / metrics-server; loosen CPU limit.
resource limits.integration: 1) Always set memory limits for apps. 2) Use CPU limits judiciously. 3) Alert on throttling/OOM. 4) Load test.

HPA.summary: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adjusts Deployment replicas based on metrics (CPU, memory, or custom).
HPA.problem: It matches capacity to load without manual scaling.
HPA.mechanics: HPA controller compares current metrics to targets and scales replicas up/down within bounds, respecting stabilization windows.
HPA.tradeoffs: Without meaningful metrics, HPA oscillates. Scale-to-zero needs KEDA/serverless patterns.
HPA.troubleshoot: Not scaling: missing metrics-server or requests unset (utilization undefined). Check hpa describe.
HPA.integration: 1) Set resource requests. 2) Install metrics-server. 3) Define min/max. 4) Load test scale behavior.

DaemonSet.summary: A DaemonSet runs a copy of a Pod on all (or selected) nodes—typical for agents/log collectors.
DaemonSet.problem: It ensures node-level agents are present without manual per-node installs.
DaemonSet.mechanics: Controller creates a Pod per matching node. Updates roll node agents. Tolerations allow scheduling on tainted nodes.
DaemonSet.tradeoffs: Not for replicated app servers—use Deployments. hostPath has security implications.
DaemonSet.troubleshoot: Missing nodes: taints without tolerations or selectors too narrow.
DaemonSet.example:
kubectl get ds -A
kubectl describe ds fluent-bit
DaemonSet.integration: 1) Deploy node agents as DaemonSets. 2) Add needed tolerations. 3) Restrict host mounts. 4) Monitor Ready nodes.

Job.summary: A Job runs Pods to completion for batch/finite tasks, retrying until backoffLimit or success.
Job.problem: It models migrations, reports, and one-shot work better than long-running Deployments.
Job.mechanics: Job creates Pods until successful completions count is met. Failures retry. CronJob creates Jobs on a schedule.
Job.tradeoffs: For continuous work use Deployments. Huge parallelism needs queue-based workers carefully.
Job.troubleshoot: Jobs stuck: inspect Pod logs and backoff. Clean finished Jobs with TTL.
Job.example:
kubectl create job migrate --from=cronjob/migrate
kubectl logs job/migrate
Job.integration: 1) Put migrations in Jobs. 2) Set backoffLimit. 3) Add TTL cleanup. 4) Alert on failed Jobs.

PersistentVolume.summary: A PersistentVolume (PV/PVC) abstracts durable storage for Pods, binding claims to volumes provisioned statically or dynamically.
PersistentVolume.problem: It keeps data beyond Pod restarts for stateful workloads.
PersistentVolume.mechanics: Pod mounts a PVC; provisioner creates a PV via StorageClass. AccessModes (RWO/RWX) constrain attach topology.
PersistentVolume.tradeoffs: RWO disks cannot multi-attach across nodes casually—use StatefulSets carefully. Snapshots/backups still required.
PersistentVolume.troubleshoot: Pending PVC: no matching StorageClass/capacity. Multi-attach errors on RWO.
PersistentVolume.example:
kubectl get pvc,pv
kubectl describe pvc data
PersistentVolume.integration: 1) Choose StorageClass. 2) Use PVCs in StatefulSets. 3) Plan backups. 4) Test restore.

NetworkPolicy.summary: NetworkPolicies restrict Pod ingress/egress traffic to allowed peers/ports (CNI-enforced).
NetworkPolicy.problem: They implement least-privilege networking inside the cluster.
NetworkPolicy.mechanics: On apply, CNI allows only matching traffic. Start with default-deny then open necessary paths.
NetworkPolicy.tradeoffs: Without a supporting CNI, policies are no-ops—verify. Over-tight policies break DNS unless egress to kube-dns allowed.
NetworkPolicy.troubleshoot: Timeouts after enabling: check DNS egress and labeled peers. Use network tools from ephemeral Pods.
NetworkPolicy.example:
policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }
NetworkPolicy.integration: 1) Confirm CNI supports policies. 2) Default deny in sensitive NS. 3) Allow DNS. 4) Expand gradually with tests.

RBAC.summary: Kubernetes RBAC authorizes users/service accounts via roles and bindings to API verbs on resources.
RBAC.problem: It enforces least privilege on the control plane API.
RBAC.mechanics: Subject authenticates; authorizer checks bindings for requested verb/resource/namespace. Prefer Role over ClusterRole when possible.
RBAC.tradeoffs: Wildcards and cluster-admin are convenient and dangerous. Audit regularly.
RBAC.troubleshoot: Forbidden errors: missing binding. Impersonation surprises: check SA used by Pods.
RBAC.integration: 1) Dedicated SA per app. 2) Minimal Roles. 3) Ban cluster-admin for apps. 4) Audit periodically.

taint/toleration.summary: Taints mark nodes so Pods won’t schedule unless they tolerate the taint; used for dedicated nodes and eviction effects.
taint/toleration.problem: They reserve nodes for special workloads (GPU, system) and control NoSchedule/NoExecute behavior.
taint/toleration.mechanics: Add taint to node; only Pods with matching toleration schedule. NoExecute can evict running non-tolerating Pods.
taint/toleration.tradeoffs: Over-tainting leaves Pods pending. Prefer affinity for soft preferences sometimes.
taint/toleration.troubleshoot: Pending with untolerated taint: add toleration or untaint. Describe Pod events.
taint/toleration.example:
kubectl taint nodes node1 dedicated=ml:NoSchedule
# Pod: tolerations: [{ key: dedicated, value: ml, effect: NoSchedule }]
taint/toleration.integration: 1) Taint special node pools. 2) Add matching tolerations only to intended workloads. 3) Document pool purpose.

control plane.summary: The Kubernetes control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler, controllers) manages cluster state and reconciliation.
control plane.problem: Worker nodes run workloads; control plane makes the decisions and stores desired state.
control plane.mechanics: kubectl talks to API server; objects persist in etcd; controllers/scheduler act on changes. Managed k8s hosts this for you.
control plane.tradeoffs: Self-managing control planes is operationally heavy—prefer managed unless required.
control plane.troubleshoot: API latency/etcd issues affect all ops—monitor control plane SLOs separately.
control plane.integration: 1) Use managed control plane if possible. 2) Monitor API/etcd health. 3) Limit API QPS from controllers. 4) Backup etcd if self-managed.

CrashLoopBackOff.summary: CrashLoopBackOff means a container repeatedly exits and kubelet backs off restart attempts.
CrashLoopBackOff.problem: It signals the process cannot stay up—config, dependency, or crash bug.
CrashLoopBackOff.mechanics: kubelet restarts crashed containers with exponential backoff. Inspect previous logs and describe events to find root cause.
CrashLoopBackOff.tradeoffs: Aggressive liveness probes can create crash loops on slow starts—tune or use startupProbe.
CrashLoopBackOff.troubleshoot: kubectl logs --previous and describe. Check command/args/env and failing migrations.
CrashLoopBackOff.example:
kubectl describe pod api-xxx
kubectl logs api-xxx --previous
CrashLoopBackOff.integration: 1) Standardize log capture. 2) Add startupProbe. 3) Fail fast with clear exit errors. 4) Alert on crash loops.

CRD/operator.summary: CustomResourceDefinitions extend the Kubernetes API; operators are controllers that reconcile those custom resources.
CRD/operator.problem: They encode operational knowledge (databases, certificates) as declarative APIs.
CRD/operator.mechanics: Install CRD; users apply CRs; operator watches and creates underlying Deployments/PVCs/etc., updating status.
CRD/operator.tradeoffs: Operators add power and failure modes—prefer mature ones. Poor operators fight humans.
CRD/operator.troubleshoot: Stuck CRs: finalizers or operator down. Check operator logs.
CRD/operator.example:
kubectl get crds
kubectl explain mydb.spec
CRD/operator.integration: 1) Adopt operators cautiously. 2) Monitor operator health. 3) Pin operator versions. 4) Document CR runbooks.

Linux filesystem hierarchy.summary: The Linux FHS places configs in /etc, variable data in /var, homes in /home, temp in /tmp, and kernel/process APIs in /proc.
Linux filesystem hierarchy.problem: Knowing the layout speeds debugging and keeps packaging predictable.
Linux filesystem hierarchy.mechanics: Apps read config from /etc, write logs/spools under /var, and expose runtime info via /proc. Containers often remount these intentionally.
Linux filesystem hierarchy.tradeoffs: Distros vary slightly; containers may be minimal without full FHS. Don't store critical state only in /tmp.
Linux filesystem hierarchy.troubleshoot: Disk full in /var: rotate logs. Missing configs: wrong path or ConfigMap mount.
Linux filesystem hierarchy.integration: 1) Follow FHS in packaging. 2) Mount /var for stateful hosts. 3) Monitor /var disk. 4) Treat /proc as API not disk.

file permissions.summary: Linux file permissions use user/group/other bits (rwx) plus ownership; modes like 644/755 are common.
file permissions.problem: They enforce least privilege on files and executables.
file permissions.mechanics: Permission checks use effective uid/gid. Directories require execute to traverse. umask sets default create masks.
file permissions.tradeoffs: ACLs add finer control; root bypasses most checks. In containers, UIDs map to host—align volumes.
file permissions.troubleshoot: EACCES: wrong owner/mode. Diagnose with namei -l and id.
file permissions.example:
ls -l file
chmod 640 file; chown app:app file
namei -l /var/app/data
file permissions.integration: 1) Run services as non-root. 2) Tighten modes. 3) Align volume UIDs. 4) Audit world-writable paths.

filesystem inode.summary: An inode stores a file’s metadata (size, perms, pointers to data blocks); directories map names→inode numbers.
filesystem inode.problem: Inode exhaustion can prevent new files even when disk space remains.
filesystem inode.mechanics: Creating a file allocates an inode and directory entry. Many tiny files can exhaust inodes on ext filesystems.
filesystem inode.tradeoffs: Some filesystems scale inodes differently; object stores avoid inode limits.
filesystem inode.troubleshoot: ‘No space’ with free bytes: df -i. Clean temp/small-file piles.
filesystem inode.integration: 1) Monitor inode usage. 2) Avoid millions of tiny files in one FS. 3) Separate volumes for such workloads.

process.summary: A Linux process is a running program with PID, memory map, FDs, and threads scheduled by the kernel.
process.problem: Process tools (ps, top, /proc) are primary for host debugging.
process.mechanics: Fork/exec create processes; they block on I/O (S), run (R), uninterruptible wait (D), or zombie (Z) until waited. Signals control lifecycle.
process.tradeoffs: Containers isolate processes via namespaces/cgroups but share a kernel.
process.troubleshoot: Zombies: parent not reaping. D-state: disk/NFS issues. Use ps and /proc.
process.example:
ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head
cat /proc/$(pgrep -n sshd)/status | head
process.integration: 1) Supervise with systemd/k8s. 2) Handle signals for graceful shutdown. 3) Alert on zombies/D-state spikes.

systemd.summary: systemd is the Linux init system managing services via unit files, dependencies, and journals.
systemd.problem: It replaces ad-hoc init scripts with declarative start/stop/restart and logging.
systemd.mechanics: systemctl start enables execution per unit; dependencies order boot. Logs go to journalctl. Restart=on-failure for crash recovery.
systemd.tradeoffs: Not all distros/containers use systemd. For containers prefer foreground processes under orchestrators.
systemd.troubleshoot: Failed units: systemctl status and journalctl -u. Remember daemon-reload after unit edits.
systemd.example:
systemctl status nginx
journalctl -u nginx -n 100 --no-pager
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
systemd.integration: 1) Package apps as units. 2) Set Restart and limits. 3) Ship journal/log shipping. 4) Reload after changes.

signal.summary: Unix signals notify processes asynchronously (SIGTERM, SIGKILL, SIGINT) for shutdown and control.
signal.problem: Graceful shutdown depends on handling SIGTERM before SIGKILL.
signal.mechanics: Kernel delivers signals; processes handle or default-terminate. Orchestrators send SIGTERM then wait then SIGKILL. In containers, PID 1 must reap and handle signals (tini).
signal.tradeoffs: SIGKILL cannot be caught—use only as last resort. Ignoring SIGTERM causes slow kills and data risk.
signal.troubleshoot: App ignores shutdown: trap signals or use init. Check docker stop grace period.
signal.example:
kill -TERM <pid>
# in shell scripts: trap 'cleanup' TERM INT
signal.integration: 1) Handle SIGTERM in apps. 2) Use proper init in containers. 3) Tune terminationGracePeriodSeconds. 4) Test rolling stops.

swap.summary: Swap extends RAM onto disk; when memory pressure hits, pages move to swap, slowing access dramatically.
swap.problem: It can prevent OOM at the cost of latency; many prod systems reduce or disable swap.
swap.mechanics: Kernel evicts cold pages to swap devices under pressure. High swap I/O (si/so) means thrashing.
swap.tradeoffs: Databases often prefer OOM over surprise swap latency. Containers may have swap disabled.
swap.troubleshoot: Latency spikes with free RAM seeming OK: check swap in/out. vmstat/si so.
swap.integration: 1) Decide swap policy per workload. 2) Alert on swap activity. 3) Size memory correctly. 4) Avoid swap for latency-critical DBs.

load average.summary: Load average is the exponential moving average of runnable (+ uninterruptible) tasks—rough system demand signal.
load average.problem: It helps spot CPU saturation or disk wait piles, interpreted relative to CPU count.
load average.mechanics: uptime reports load; compare to core count. High load with low CPU may be disk/network D-state tasks.
load average.tradeoffs: Load alone lacks causality—pair with CPU%, iowait, and latency SLIs.
load average.troubleshoot: Investigate with top/vmstat/iostat when load >> cores.
load average.integration: 1) Chart load vs CPUs. 2) Correlate with latency. 3) Split CPU vs IO causes. 4) Scale or fix bottlenecks.

memory pressure.summary: Memory pressure means free memory is low and the kernel is reclaiming caches/swap or approaching OOM.
memory pressure.problem: It degrades performance and can kill processes via OOM killer.
memory pressure.mechanics: Watch MemAvailable, cgroup usage vs limit, and OOM events. Reduce caches, fix leaks, or raise limits/scale.
memory pressure.tradeoffs: Over-provisioning wastes money; under-provisioning causes kills. Measure working set under load.
memory pressure.troubleshoot: OOMKilled containers: kubectl describe / dmesg. Host pressure: free -h and psi if available.
memory pressure.integration: 1) Set container memory limits. 2) Alert on pressure/OOM. 3) Fix leaks. 4) Load test memory.

memory leak.summary: A memory leak retains unused memory (references or native allocs) until RSS grows without bound.
memory leak.problem: It eventually causes OOM, thrashing, or eviction.
memory leak.mechanics: Profile heap to find retained paths; watch RSS growth slope. Restarts mitigate but don't fix.
memory leak.tradeoffs: Unbounded caches look like leaks—cap them. Language GC heaps vs native (off-heap) differ.
memory leak.troubleshoot: Capture heap dump under load; compare baselines. Check cgroup OOM events.
memory leak.example:
# Node example mindset: clinic heap / --inspect heap snapshot
# Go: pprof heap
memory leak.integration: 1) Cap caches. 2) Continuous RSS graphs. 3) Profile before paging. 4) Fix root cause, not only restart.

high CPU.summary: High CPU means processes saturate cores, increasing latency and load average.
high CPU.problem: It signals hot loops, tight polls, or insufficient capacity.
high CPU.mechanics: Identify top PIDs (top/pidstat), profile (perf/pprof), fix algorithmic hotspots or scale out. Distinguish GC/system time.
high CPU.tradeoffs: CPU limits in containers throttle before node saturation. Scale horizontally when work is parallel.
high CPU.troubleshoot: Correlate with deploy times. Use flame graphs for sustained highs.
high CPU.integration: 1) Alert on CPU saturation. 2) Profile hot paths. 3) Fix or scale. 4) Review limit throttling.

Bash strict mode.summary: Bash strict mode commonly means set -euo pipefail (and often IFS) to fail fast on errors, unset vars, and pipeline failures.
Bash strict mode.problem: It prevents scripts from continuing after silent failures.
Bash strict mode.mechanics: Enable at script top; handle expected nonzero exits explicitly. Use traps for cleanup.
Bash strict mode.tradeoffs: Strict mode can be surprising with pipelines/greps—set allowances carefully.
Bash strict mode.troubleshoot: Script exits early: check which command failed with -x tracing.
Bash strict mode.integration: 1) Template all scripts with strict mode. 2) CI-lint shell. 3) Add -x in debug. 4) Prefer Python for complex logic.

shell pipeline.summary: A shell pipeline connects stdout of one command to stdin of the next with | for compositional text processing.
shell pipeline.problem: It enables powerful one-liners without temp files.
shell pipeline.mechanics: Commands run concurrently connected by pipes. Without pipefail, pipeline status is last command only.
shell pipeline.tradeoffs: Huge streams need care; prefer awk/SQL for heavy joins. Quoting matters.
shell pipeline.troubleshoot: Wrong results: encoding/sort locale. Debug stages separately.
shell pipeline.example: cat access.log | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head
shell pipeline.integration: 1) Use pipefail. 2) Quote variables. 3) Break complex pipes into scripts. 4) Test on sample logs.

continuous integration.summary: CI automatically builds and tests every change to keep the main branch integrable and green.
continuous integration.problem: It catches breakages early and reduces merge hell.
continuous integration.mechanics: Push/PR triggers workflows: checkout, build, test, lint. Failures block merge. Cache dependencies by lockfile hash.
continuous integration.tradeoffs: Slow/flaky CI reduces trust—invest in stability. CD builds on CI artifacts.
continuous integration.troubleshoot: Flakes: quarantine with owners. Cache misses: verify keys.
continuous integration.example:
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci && npm test
continuous integration.integration: 1) Require CI on protected branches. 2) Keep under ~10–15 min. 3) Kill flakes. 4) Cache deps.

continuous delivery.summary: Continuous delivery keeps software releasable so deploying to prod is a routine, automated, low-risk action.
continuous delivery.problem: It shortens lead time from commit to production value.
continuous delivery.mechanics: CI produces artifacts; CD pipelines deploy to staging/prod with gates. Feature flags and canaries reduce risk.
continuous delivery.tradeoffs: Continuous deployment auto-goes to prod; continuous delivery ensures you could. Choose based on risk appetite.
continuous delivery.troubleshoot: Failed deploys: artifact mismatch, config drift, health checks. Keep one-click rollback.
continuous delivery.example: # promote the same image digest staging → prod
continuous delivery.integration: 1) Deploy same artifact across envs. 2) Automate smoke tests. 3) Add rollback. 4) Measure lead time.

workflow.summary: A GitHub Actions workflow is a YAML-defined automation triggered by events, containing jobs and steps.
workflow.problem: It encodes CI/CD and repo automation as code.
workflow.mechanics: Event triggers workflow; jobs run on runners (possibly parallel); steps execute actions/commands. Least-privilege permissions recommended.
workflow.tradeoffs: Reusable workflows reduce duplication. Self-hosted runners need hardening.
workflow.troubleshoot: Pending jobs: runner labels/availability. Secrets: check environments.
workflow.example:
name: ci
on: { pull_request: { branches: [main] } }
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [{ uses: actions/checkout@v4 }, { run: make test }]
workflow.integration: 1) Put workflows in .github/workflows. 2) Pin action versions. 3) Restrict permissions. 4) Require for merges.

runner.summary: A runner is the machine/VM that executes CI jobs (GitHub-hosted or self-hosted).
runner.problem: Job capacity and isolation depend on runner pools.
runner.mechanics: Orchestrator assigns jobs to matching-labeled runners; they checkout and execute steps. Ephemeral runners reduce persistence risk.
runner.tradeoffs: Self-hosted is cheaper/heavier and must be locked down. Hosted is simpler with limits.
runner.troubleshoot: Queueing: scale runners or reduce job time. Dirty workspaces: prefer clean ephemeral.
runner.example:
runs-on: ubuntu-latest
# or: [self-hosted, linux, x64, gpu]
runner.integration: 1) Prefer hosted until scale demands. 2) Harden self-hosted. 3) Use ephemeral where possible. 4) Monitor queue time.

reusable workflow.summary: Reusable workflows are callable workflow YAMLs that centralize shared CI/CD logic across repos.
reusable workflow.problem: They reduce copy-paste drift in org pipelines.
reusable workflow.mechanics: Caller uses jobs.<id>.uses: org/repo/.github/workflows/x.yml@ref with inputs. Pin refs for stability.
reusable workflow.tradeoffs: Over-centralizing creates bottlenecks—version carefully. Actions vs reusable workflows solve different reuse levels.
reusable workflow.troubleshoot: Breakages cascade—canary the reusable workflow version.
reusable workflow.integration: 1) Extract common CI. 2) Version tags. 3) Document inputs. 4) Roll forward deliberately.

pipeline artifact.summary: Pipeline artifacts are build outputs (binaries, images, reports) stored for later jobs/deploys.
pipeline artifact.problem: They ensure the same bits tested are the bits deployed.
pipeline artifact.mechanics: Build job uploads artifact or pushes image digest; deploy job consumes that exact artifact—not a rebuild.
pipeline artifact.tradeoffs: Rebuilding per environment risks drift. Retain enough history for rollback audits.
pipeline artifact.troubleshoot: Missing artifacts: expired retention or wrong names. Verify digests.
pipeline artifact.example:
- uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
  with: { name: web-dist, path: dist/ }
pipeline artifact.integration: 1) Publish artifacts once. 2) Deploy by digest. 3) Set retention. 4) Sign critical artifacts.

build cache.summary: CI build caches store dependencies/intermediate build outputs keyed by lockfiles to speed pipelines.
build cache.problem: They cut wall-clock time and registry load.
build cache.mechanics: On hit, restore cache before install/build; on miss, populate. Key by OS + lockfile hash. Docker BuildKit cache exports similarly.
build cache.tradeoffs: Stale caches can hide bugs—periodically clean. Never cache secrets.
build cache.troubleshoot: Low hit rate: unstable keys or matrix sprawl. Inspect key computation.
build cache.example:
- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: ~/.npm
    key: ${{ runner.os }}-npm-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
build cache.integration: 1) Cache package dirs. 2) Key by lockfiles. 3) Enable BuildKit cache. 4) Monitor hit rates.

merge.summary: Merging integrates a completed branch into the target (often via PR squash/merge/rebase strategies).
merge.problem: Controlled merges protect main while integrating reviewed work.
merge.mechanics: CI green + approvals → merge strategy updates main. Branch protection enforces rules.
merge.tradeoffs: Squash simplifies history; merge commits preserve branch topology. Pick one org standard.
merge.troubleshoot: Blocked merges: failing checks or rulesets. Resolve conflicts locally first.
merge.integration: 1) Protect main. 2) Require CI+reviews. 3) Standardize merge style. 4) Delete merged branches.

Auto Scaling.summary: Auto Scaling adds/removes instances based on metrics so capacity tracks demand.
Auto Scaling.problem: It improves availability and cost efficiency versus static fleets.
Auto Scaling.mechanics: Cloud service watches metrics (CPU/ALB requests); when thresholds breach, it launches/terminates instances in the group and registers with the load balancer.
Auto Scaling.tradeoffs: Reactive scaling lags spikes; schedule + predictive help. Misconfigured health checks churn instances.
Auto Scaling.troubleshoot: Flapping: widen thresholds/cooldowns. Not scaling: IAM, metrics gaps, or wrong ASG attachment.
Auto Scaling.integration: 1) Put instances behind LB in an ASG. 2) Scale on meaningful SLI proxies. 3) Set min≥2 for HA. 4) Load test.

CloudWatch.summary: CloudWatch is AWS’s monitoring service for metrics, logs, and alarms on AWS resources and custom app metrics.
CloudWatch.problem: It provides the basic observability plane for AWS-native stacks.
CloudWatch.mechanics: Agents/services emit metrics/logs; you alarm on thresholds and route to SNS. Custom metrics via PutMetricData/EMF.
CloudWatch.tradeoffs: Prometheus may fit multi-cloud/k8s better; CloudWatch is integrated and simple for AWS.
CloudWatch.troubleshoot: Missing metrics: namespaces/dimensions wrong or no permissions. High cost: verbose logs—sample/filter.
CloudWatch.example: aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name high-cpu --metric-name CPUUtilization --namespace AWS/EC2 --threshold 80 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold --evaluation-periods 2 --statistic Average --period 60 --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-…
CloudWatch.integration: 1) Define golden signals. 2) Create alarms to paging. 3) Centralize logs. 4) Cap retention.

EC2.summary: EC2 provides resizable virtual machines (instances) in AWS with chosen AMI, size, network, and storage.
EC2.problem: It is the general-purpose compute building block for lift-and-shift and custom runtimes.
EC2.mechanics: Launch from AMI into a subnet with SG/IAM role; user data bootstraps. Prefer SSM over SSH when possible.
EC2.tradeoffs: Lambda/Fargate reduce ops for many apps; EC2 wins for specialized kernels/GPUs/long processes.
EC2.troubleshoot: Unreachable: SG/NACL/route. Use instance connect/SSM. Check status checks.
EC2.integration: 1) Standardize AMIs. 2) Use IAM roles not keys. 3) Force IMDSv2. 4) Autoscale when needed.

ELB/ALB.summary: Elastic Load Balancing (ALB/NLB/CLB) distributes traffic across targets; ALB is L7 HTTP-aware.
ELB/ALB.problem: It enables HA, TLS termination, and path-based routing.
ELB/ALB.mechanics: Client hits listener; ALB routes by rules to healthy targets in target groups. Health checks remove bad targets.
ELB/ALB.tradeoffs: NLB for L4/extreme performance; ALB for HTTP routing. Mis-healthchecks cause outages.
ELB/ALB.troubleshoot: 5xx: bad targets or timeouts. Check target health and SG between ALB and instances.
ELB/ALB.integration: 1) Place ALB public/private intentionally. 2) Tune health checks. 3) Attach ASG. 4) Alert on unhealthy hosts.

IAM user.summary: An IAM user is a long-lived AWS identity with access keys/passwords—generally discouraged for apps vs roles.
IAM user.problem: Users exist for humans/break-glass; workloads should use roles.
IAM user.mechanics: Attach policies to user/group; humans use console with MFA; avoid embedding access keys in servers.
IAM user.tradeoffs: Roles with temporary creds are safer for apps. SSO federation beats many IAM users.
IAM user.troubleshoot: Leaked keys: deactivate immediately, cloudtrail review. Rotate and prefer roles.
IAM user.integration: 1) Human users via SSO. 2) MFA everywhere. 3) No static keys on servers. 4) Audit unused credentials.

Internet Gateway.summary: An Internet Gateway (IGW) is a VPC component that enables bidirectional Internet connectivity for resources with public IPs.
Internet Gateway.problem: Without an IGW and correct routes, public subnets cannot reach/be reached from the Internet.
Internet Gateway.mechanics: Attach IGW to VPC; route public subnet 0.0.0.0/0 to IGW; assign public IPs. Private subnets use NAT for egress only.
Internet Gateway.tradeoffs: NAT Gateway provides outbound-only for private subnets. Don't put data stores in public subnets casually.
Internet Gateway.troubleshoot: No Internet: missing IGW route, public IP, or NACL/SG. Trace route tables.
Internet Gateway.integration: 1) Attach one IGW per VPC. 2) Route only public subnets to IGW. 3) Prefer private+NAT for apps. 4) Lock SGs.

NAT.summary: A NAT Gateway/instance allows private-subnet egress to the Internet without accepting inbound connections.
NAT.problem: It lets private instances pull packages/APIs while remaining non-public.
NAT.mechanics: Private subnet route 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT in a public subnet; NAT SNAT outbound. Use per-AZ NATs for HA.
NAT.tradeoffs: NAT costs money and can bottleneck; VPC endpoints reduce need for AWS API egress.
NAT.troubleshoot: Egress fails: wrong route, SG, or NAT down. Check CloudWatch NAT metrics.
NAT.integration: 1) Place NAT in public subnet. 2) Point private routes to it. 3) Multi-AZ for prod. 4) Prefer endpoints for AWS APIs.

RDS.summary: RDS is AWS managed relational databases (Postgres/MySQL/etc.) handling patching, backups, and Multi-AZ failover options.
RDS.problem: It reduces undifferentiated DB operations versus self-managed EC2 databases.
RDS.mechanics: Provision instance/cluster in private subnets; apps connect via endpoint; Multi-AZ sync standby for failover; backups enable PITR.
RDS.tradeoffs: Aurora vs RDS trade cost/features. Superuser access limited vs self-managed.
RDS.troubleshoot: Connectivity: SG/DNS. Failover: DNS tip; use retries. Storage full alerts.
RDS.integration: 1) Private subnets only. 2) Enable Multi-AZ for prod. 3) Automate parameter changes carefully. 4) Test failover.

Route 53.summary: Route 53 is AWS DNS: public/private hosted zones, health checks, and routing policies (weighted/failover/latency).
Route 53.problem: It controls how names resolve for users and internal services.
Route 53.mechanics: Create zone/records; set TTL; Alias records point to ALB/CloudFront without IPv4 management. Health checks drive failover policies.
Route 53.tradeoffs: External DNS can work too; Route 53 integrates with AWS targets. Low TTL helps failover but increases queries.
Route 53.troubleshoot: Stale DNS after cutover: TTL caches. Compare dig results globally.
Route 53.integration: 1) Manage zones as code. 2) Plan TTLs before migrations. 3) Use health-checked failover. 4) Monitor query fails.

S3.summary: S3 is durable object storage for blobs with buckets, keys, versioning, and IAM policies.
S3.problem: It stores backups, static assets, data lakes, and artifacts cheaply at scale.
S3.mechanics: PutObject stores by key; GET retrieves. Use least-privilege IAM, block public access by default, lifecycle to IA/Glacier.
S3.tradeoffs: Not a POSIX filesystem—no partial append semantics like disks. Cross-region replication for DR.
S3.troubleshoot: AccessDenied: policy/KMS. Unexpected public: audit ACLs/policies.
S3.integration: 1) Block public access. 2) Encrypt. 3) Version critical buckets. 4) Lifecycle + monitoring.

VPC.summary: A VPC is an isolated virtual network in AWS with CIDRs, subnets, route tables, and gateways.
VPC.problem: It is the foundation for placing compute and controlling network paths.
VPC.mechanics: Create VPC+subnets across AZs; attach IGW/NAT; place resources; use SGs/NACLs. Endpoints reach AWS APIs privately.
VPC.tradeoffs: Overlapping CIDRs break peering/VPN. Plan ranges early.
VPC.troubleshoot: No connectivity: routes/SG/NACL/DNS. Use Reachability Analyzer.
VPC.integration: 1) Plan non-overlapping CIDRs. 2) Multi-AZ subnets. 3) Private apps. 4) Codify in Terraform.

public subnet.summary: A public subnet has a route to an Internet Gateway and typically assigns public IPs to instances.
public subnet.problem: It hosts Internet-facing load balancers/bastions—not databases.
public subnet.mechanics: Route table 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW. Prefer placing only LBs/NAT there; apps in private subnets.
public subnet.tradeoffs: Public EC2 increases attack surface—prefer private + LB.
public subnet.troubleshoot: Instances lack Internet: missing public IP or IGW route.
public subnet.integration: 1) Mark subnets clearly. 2) Only edge components public. 3) Strict SGs. 4) Monitor exposed ports.

security group.summary: A security group is a stateful virtual firewall around AWS ENIs allowing explicit inbound/outbound rules.
security group.problem: It is the primary microservice network control in AWS.
security group.mechanics: Attach SG to ENI; add least-privilege ports from specific CIDRs/SGs. Responses allowed automatically (stateful).
security group.tradeoffs: NACLs are stateless subnet-level. Prefer SG references over wide CIDRs.
security group.troubleshoot: Timeouts: missing ingress on server or egress on client. Diff rules in console/IaC.
security group.example: aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-… --protocol tcp --port 5432 --source-group sg-app
security group.integration: 1) Default deny inbound. 2) Reference SGs. 3) Manage via IaC. 4) Regular rule audits.

region.summary: An AWS Region is a geographic area of isolated Availability Zones; choose for latency, data residency, and DR.
region.problem: Resources are regional; cross-region needs explicit replication.
region.mechanics: Deploy into a region; use multiple AZs for HA. Replicate to another region for DR if required.
region.tradeoffs: Multi-region is powerful and costly/complex. Start multi-AZ single region.
region.troubleshoot: Wrong region in CLI: configure profile. Service missing in region: check docs.
region.example:
aws configure get region
aws ec2 describe-availability-zones
region.integration: 1) Pick primary region. 2) Multi-AZ. 3) Document DR region strategy. 4) Pin region in IaC.

IaaS.summary: IaaS provides virtualized compute/storage/network building blocks you configure (VMs, disks, VPCs).
IaaS.problem: It maximizes control versus PaaS/SaaS while shifting more ops onto you.
IaaS.mechanics: Provision VMs/networks; you patch OS and run apps. Cloud still manages hardware/hypervisor.
IaaS.tradeoffs: PaaS faster for apps; IaaS for custom networking/OS. Mix via containers on IaaS.
IaaS.troubleshoot: Ownership gaps cause vulnerabilities—clarify patch duties.
IaaS.integration: 1) Decide IaaS vs PaaS per component. 2) Automate patching. 3) Codify infra. 4) Apply CIS baselines.

Infrastructure as Code.summary: IaC defines infrastructure in versioned declarative code (Terraform/CloudFormation) applied repeatedly.
Infrastructure as Code.problem: It makes environments reproducible and reviewable.
Infrastructure as Code.mechanics: Write configs; plan shows diff; apply mutates cloud APIs; state tracks ownership.
Infrastructure as Code.tradeoffs: ClickOps drifts from code—import or recreate. Huge monoliths of IaC hurt; modularize.
Infrastructure as Code.troubleshoot: State conflicts: use remote state locking. Unexpected destroys: careful plan review.
Infrastructure as Code.integration: 1) Put all prod infra in IaC. 2) PR reviews for plans. 3) Remote state+lock. 4) CI plan on PR.

idempotence.summary: Idempotence means applying an operation multiple times yields the same result without unintended duplicates.
idempotence.problem: It makes automation safe to retry under failure.
idempotence.mechanics: Design APIs/automation so repeats are no-ops or reinforce desired state (create-if-not-exists).
idempotence.tradeoffs: True perfect idempotence can be hard with side effects—use idempotency keys.
idempotence.example: # HTTP: PUT /users/42 with full body is more idempotent than POST /users
idempotence.integration: 1) Prefer declarative tools. 2) Add unique constraints. 3) Idempotency keys for payments. 4) Retry safely.

inventory.summary: Ansible inventory lists hosts/groups and variables defining automation targets.
inventory.problem: It scopes playbooks to the right machines.
inventory.mechanics: Inventory provides connection info; playbooks select hosts. Dynamic inventory pulls from cloud APIs.
inventory.tradeoffs: Dynamic scales better for cloud churn; static is simple for labs.
inventory.troubleshoot: Wrong hosts changed: check group patterns and limits.
inventory.integration: 1) Source inventory dynamically in cloud. 2) Separate env inventories. 3) Limit by group. 4) Audit vars.

role.summary: An Ansible role packages tasks, handlers, templates, and defaults into a reusable unit.
role.problem: It modularizes playbooks for shareable configuration.
role.mechanics: Playbooks include roles; roles apply tasks idempotently and notify handlers on change.
role.tradeoffs: Roles vs collections: collections distribute broader content. Keep roles focused.
role.troubleshoot: Unexpected changes: var precedence. Use --check and diff.
role.integration: 1) Extract repeated tasks into roles. 2) Version roles. 3) Test with molecule if possible. 4) Pin versions.

backup.summary: Backups copy data so you can restore after loss/corruption; they must be tested.
backup.problem: They are the last line of defense when replication isn't enough (logical bugs).
backup.mechanics: Schedule backups; store offsite/immutable; periodically restore to verify. Align with RPO/RTO.
backup.tradeoffs: Snapshots ≠ complete DR without application consistency. Replication doesn't protect against bad writes.
backup.troubleshoot: Restore fails: missing credentials or incomplete sets—practice restores.
backup.example: aws backup start-backup-job …  # or pg_dump/pg_basebackup depending on system
backup.integration: 1) Define RPO/RTO. 2) Automate backups. 3) Quarterly restore drills. 4) Monitor job failures.

RPO.summary: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time.
RPO.problem: It drives backup frequency and replication design.
RPO.mechanics: If RPO is 5 minutes, you need continuous or frequent backups/replication within that lag.
RPO.tradeoffs: Tighter RPO costs more. Business sets RPO; engineering implements.
RPO.troubleshoot: Missed RPO: lagging replicas or failed backups—alert on lag/age.
RPO.example: # RPO 15m → backups or sync every ≤15m with margin
RPO.integration: 1) Get business RPO. 2) Implement accordingly. 3) Alert on backup age/lag. 4) Document per system.

canary deployment.summary: Canary deployment releases a new version to a small traffic slice before full rollout.
canary deployment.problem: It limits blast radius while gathering real-user signal.
canary deployment.mechanics: Deploy canary instances; shift 1–5% traffic; watch errors/latency; promote or abort.
canary deployment.tradeoffs: Requires good metrics and traffic splitting (mesh/LB). Feature flags are an alternative.
canary deployment.troubleshoot: False confidence: insufficient traffic. Bad metrics: wrong SLIs.
canary deployment.example: # FLB weighted target groups or service mesh traffic split
canary deployment.integration: 1) Define success SLIs. 2) Automate canary analysis. 3) Instant rollback path. 4) Start with low %.

rollback.summary: Rollback reverts to a prior known-good version/config after a bad deploy.
rollback.problem: It is the fastest mitigation when forward-fix would take too long.
rollback.mechanics: Redeploy prior image/manifest revision; ensure schema is backward compatible or use expand/contract migrations.
rollback.tradeoffs: Some failures need forward fixes (bad data migrations). Practice rollbacks.
rollback.example:
kubectl rollout undo deploy/api
helm rollback myapp 1
rollback.integration: 1) Keep prior artifacts. 2) Compatible migrations. 3) One-command rollback. 4) Game-day practice.

rolling deployment.summary: Rolling deployment replaces instances gradually with the new version while keeping service available.
rolling deployment.problem: It avoids full downtime of big-bang replaces.
rolling deployment.mechanics: Take down/replace a subset, wait healthy, continue. Orchestrators encode surge/unavailable parameters.
rolling deployment.tradeoffs: Canaries add safety; blue/green doubles capacity. Slow rolls prolong mixed versions.
rolling deployment.troubleshoot: Stuck rolls: failing readiness. Pause and inspect.
rolling deployment.integration: 1) Use readiness probes. 2) Tune surge/unavailable. 3) Monitor during roll. 4) Abort on SLI breach.

health check.summary: Health checks probe whether an instance should receive traffic or be replaced.
health check.problem: They keep load balancers and orchestrators honest about readiness.
health check.mechanics: LB/orchestrator calls HTTP/TCP endpoint; failures remove/restart targets. Keep checks cheap and accurate.
health check.tradeoffs: Deep checks can cascade outages if they depend on downstreams—prefer shallow + separate ready.
health check.troubleshoot: Flapping: loosen thresholds. Always-unhealthy: wrong path/port.
health check.integration: 1) Implement /healthz and /readyz. 2) Wire to LB/k8s. 3) Avoid expensive dependency fanout. 4) Alert on failing checks.

GitOps.summary: GitOps uses Git as the source of truth for desired cluster/app state, continuously reconciled by an agent.
GitOps.problem: It provides auditability and consistent delivery.
GitOps.mechanics: Commit manifests; controller applies and reverts drift. Changes go through PR review.
GitOps.tradeoffs: Secrets need sealing/ESO. Not every infra change fits pure GitOps.
GitOps.troubleshoot: Out-of-sync: check controller logs and Git permissions.
GitOps.integration: 1) Store manifests in Git. 2) Install reconciler. 3) Protect main. 4) Monitor sync status.

OpenTofu.summary: OpenTofu is an open-source Terraform fork for declarative infrastructure provisioning with HCL and providers.
OpenTofu.problem: It provides community-governed IaC compatible with Terraform workflows.
OpenTofu.mechanics: Write HCL; init providers; plan; apply; state tracks resources. Remote backends + locking for teams.
OpenTofu.tradeoffs: Terraform Cloud vs OpenTofu/CLI trade support models. Pin provider versions.
OpenTofu.troubleshoot: State lock stuck: release carefully after ensuring no apply running.
OpenTofu.integration: 1) Standardize on OpenTofu or Terraform. 2) Remote state. 3) CI plans. 4) Module versioning.

plan.summary: terraform/tofu plan computes the diff between desired config and state without applying.
plan.problem: It is the safety review step before mutating cloud resources.
plan.mechanics: plan refreshes state, walks graph, prints actions. Review destroys carefully; apply exact saved plan in CI.
plan.tradeoffs: Plans can be stale if state changes underneath—lock and apply promptly.
plan.troubleshoot: Unexpected destroys: renamed resources without moved blocks.
plan.integration: 1) Require plan artifacts in PRs. 2) Human review destroys. 3) Apply saved plans. 4) Use `moved` blocks.

state.summary: Terraform/OpenTofu state maps configuration addresses to real cloud resource IDs.
state.problem: Without state, tools cannot reliably update or destroy the right resources.
state.mechanics: After apply, state stores IDs/attributes. Remote state (S3+Dynamo, etc.) enables teams.
state.tradeoffs: Never hand-edit casually. Sensitive data in state needs encrypted backends.
state.troubleshoot: Orphan resources: state lost—import or adopt. Drift: refresh/plan.
state.integration: 1) Remote encrypted state. 2) Restrict access. 3) Backup state. 4) Avoid manual edits.

state locking.summary: State locking prevents concurrent applies from corrupting Terraform state.
state locking.mechanics: Backend acquires lock before plan/apply; others wait/fail. Force-unlock only if process is dead.
state locking.tradeoffs: Local state lacks safe team locking—don't use for prod teams.
state locking.troubleshoot: Stuck lock: verify no runner active then unlock.
state locking.example: # S3 backend with dynamodb_table for locks
state locking.integration: 1) Enable locking backend. 2) CI uses same backend. 3) Never unlock blindly. 4) Alert on long locks.

remote state.summary: Remote state stores Terraform state in shared durable storage (S3, GCS, Terraform Cloud).
remote state.problem: It enables collaboration and state locking.
remote state.mechanics: Configure backend; terraform init migrates; team shares one state per workspace carefully.
remote state.tradeoffs: One state per environment/app boundary—avoid mega-states.
remote state.troubleshoot: AccessDenied: IAM on backend. Enable versioning for recovery.
remote state.integration: 1) Create encrypted versioned bucket. 2) Configure backend. 3) Lock table. 4) Limit IAM read/write.

module.summary: A Terraform module is a reusable packaged set of resources with inputs/outputs.
module.problem: It standardizes patterns (VPC, ECS service) across environments.
module.mechanics: Root module calls child modules with variables; outputs feed other modules. Pin module versions.
module.tradeoffs: Over-abstracted modules become opaque. Start concrete, extract later.
module.troubleshoot: Version drift: pin and renovate intentionally.
module.integration: 1) Extract repeated infra. 2) Semantic-version modules. 3) Document inputs. 4) Test examples.

resource.summary: A Terraform resource block declares one infrastructure object managed by a provider.
resource.problem: Resources are the atomic units of IaC desired state.
resource.mechanics: Provider maps resource to API calls create/read/update/delete. Implicit deps via references; explicit depends_on rarely.
resource.tradeoffs: Data sources read without owning. Avoid provisioners when possible.
resource.integration: 1) One logical object per resource. 2) Use lifecycle guards. 3) Prefer managed attrs over local-exec. 4) Review force-new diffs.

import.summary: terraform import adopts an existing cloud object into state under a resource address.
import.problem: It brings ClickOps resources under IaC without recreate.
import.mechanics: Write matching config; import ID into state; plan until clean. Newer workflows can generate config.
import.tradeoffs: Import doesn't change cloud—only state. Mis-import mismanages resources.
import.troubleshoot: Plans want destroy/recreate: attributes mismatch—align config.
import.integration: 1) Write config first. 2) Import. 3) Plan to zero. 4) Commit.

drift.summary: Drift is when real infrastructure differs from IaC desired state due to manual changes or out-of-band edits.
drift.problem: It causes surprises on next apply and undermines audits.
drift.mechanics: Detect via periodic plans or drift tools; reconcile by apply or updating code. Lock down console permissions.
drift.tradeoffs: Some drift is inevitable (autoscaled counts)—ignore_changes selectively.
drift.troubleshoot: Unexpected diffs: find who changed via CloudTrail.
drift.integration: 1) Limit console IAM. 2) Nightly plans. 3) ignore_changes only when justified. 4) Educate on GitOps/IaC.

chart.summary: A Helm chart packages Kubernetes manifests with templates and default values for installable apps.
chart.problem: It standardizes deploying complex software to clusters.
chart.mechanics: helm install renders templates with values and applies. Upgrades revise release; rollback uses revision history.
chart.tradeoffs: Kustomize is alternative without templating engine. Charts can hide risky defaults—read values.
chart.troubleshoot: Failed release: helm status/logs. Values typos common.
chart.integration: 1) Vendor charts carefully. 2) Pin versions. 3) Manage values in Git. 4) Test upgrades.

values.summary: Helm values are configuration inputs that parameterize chart templates per environment.
values.problem: They keep one chart reusable across stages.
values.mechanics: Defaults ship in chart; env overlays override. Avoid --set for complex structures; use files.
values.tradeoffs: Secrets in values need sealing/SOPS—not plain Git.
values.troubleshoot: Wrong env deployed: check which values file. helm get values.
values.integration: 1) Layer values per env. 2) Validate schema. 3) Encrypt secrets. 4) Diff before upgrade.

PromQL.summary: PromQL is Prometheus’s query language for selecting and aggregating time-series metrics.
PromQL.problem: It powers alerts and dashboards on golden signals.
PromQL.mechanics: Select series by labels; apply rate on counters; aggregate with sum/avg by. Keep label cardinality bounded.
PromQL.tradeoffs: High cardinality explodes memory. Prefer recording rules for heavy queries.
PromQL.troubleshoot: Empty graphs: label mismatch or scrape gaps.
PromQL.integration: 1) Define SLI queries. 2) Build alerts. 3) Control labels. 4) Use recording rules.

scrape model.summary: Prometheus primarily scrapes metrics from targets’ HTTP endpoints on an interval (pull model).
scrape model.problem: It decentralizes instrumentation and simplifies target discovery.
scrape model.mechanics: Prometheus discovers targets, scrapes exposition format, stores samples. Apps expose /metrics.
scrape model.tradeoffs: Push is exceptional (batch jobs via Pushgateway). Short-lived pods need careful discovery.
scrape model.troubleshoot: Missing targets: SD/relabel config. Check /targets page.
scrape model.integration: 1) Expose /metrics. 2) Configure scrape jobs. 3) Use k8s SD. 4) Monitor scrape health.

metric.summary: A metric is a numeric time series measuring system behavior (counters, gauges, histograms).
metric.problem: Metrics enable SLIs, capacity planning, and alerting.
metric.mechanics: Instrument code; export; scrape/store; query. Prefer RED/USE golden signals.
metric.tradeoffs: Logs/traces complement metrics. Too many labels kill Prometheus.
metric.troubleshoot: Weird spikes: check resets on counters—use rate().
metric.integration: 1) Agree on golden metrics. 2) Instrument services. 3) Bound labels. 4) Alert on SLIs.

dashboard.summary: Dashboards visualize metrics/logs for situational awareness during operations and incidents.
dashboard.problem: They compress many signals into human-scanable views.
dashboard.mechanics: Build from SLIs first; template by service; avoid vanity charts. Prefer RED panels for request services.
dashboard.troubleshoot: Empty panels: datasource permissions or label drift.
dashboard.example: # Grafana: rate(errors)/rate(requests) as error ratio panel
dashboard.integration: 1) Create service overview dashboards. 2) Standard variables. 3) Link alerts→panels. 4) Review quarterly.

trace.summary: Distributed traces follow a request across services via span context (OpenTelemetry/Jaeger/Zipkin).
trace.problem: They diagnose latency attribution in microservice calls.
trace.mechanics: Each service creates spans; propagates headers; backend assembles traces. Sample to control cost.
trace.tradeoffs: 100% sampling is expensive. Metrics still needed for SLOs.
trace.troubleshoot: Broken traces: missing propagation headers across hops.
trace.integration: 1) Adopt OpenTelemetry SDKs. 2) Propagate context. 3) Sample wisely. 4) Tie traces to exemplars.

instrumentation.summary: Instrumentation adds metrics/logs/traces to code so systems are observable.
instrumentation.mechanics: Add SDK/auto-instrumentation; export to backends; standardize attributes (service.name).
instrumentation.tradeoffs: Too much instrumentation noise/cost—focus on user journeys.
instrumentation.troubleshoot: Missing data: exporter config/endpoints. Verify with a known request.
instrumentation.example:
from opentelemetry import trace
tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__)
instrumentation.integration: 1) Standardize OTel. 2) Auto-instrument frameworks. 3) Add custom spans for critical paths. 4) Review cardinality.

SLI.summary: An SLI (Service Level Indicator) is a quantitative measure of user-facing reliability (availability, latency).
SLI.problem: It makes reliability measurable rather than anecdotal.
SLI.mechanics: Define event and good predicate; compute ratio over window. Example: non-5xx requests / total.
SLI.tradeoffs: Vanity metrics aren't SLIs. Choose indicators users feel.
SLI.troubleshoot: SLI flat wrong: bad event definition or sampling bias.
SLI.integration: 1) Pick 1–3 SLIs per critical journey. 2) Implement queries. 3) Chart burn. 4) Review with product.

SLO.summary: An SLO (Service Level Objective) sets a target on an SLI over a window (e.g., 99.9% monthly).
SLO.problem: It balances feature velocity vs reliability via error budgets.
SLO.mechanics: Choose target from user needs/cost; track compliance; alert on budget burn rate, not raw blips.
SLO.tradeoffs: Too tight SLOs stall delivery; too loose hide pain. Iterate.
SLO.troubleshoot: Chronic miss: invest in reliability or renegotiate SLO.
SLO.integration: 1) Set SLOs with stakeholders. 2) Track budget. 3) Multi-window burn alerts. 4) Freeze risky launches when budget exhausted.

error budget.summary: Error budget is the allowed unreliability derived from an SLO (1 - objective) over the window.
error budget.problem: It quantifies how much risk/failure you can spend on change.
error budget.mechanics: Measure consumed budget from SLI; high burn triggers pages; exhausted budget pauses risky deploys.
error budget.tradeoffs: Budgets only work with enforcement culture. Don't reset silently.
error budget.troubleshoot: Unexpected burn: partial outages or bad SLI. Investigate.
error budget.example: # burn rate 2× means budget depletes in half the window
error budget.integration: 1) Compute budget. 2) Alert on burn. 3) Write policy. 4) Review monthly.

toil.summary: Toil is manual, repetitive, automatable operational work that scales with service size (SRE definition).
toil.problem: Reducing toil frees engineering time for durable improvements.
toil.mechanics: Track toil; automate runbooks; create self-service platforms. Measure on-call ticket types.
toil.tradeoffs: Some ops work is necessary engineering—not all ops is toil.
toil.troubleshoot: Rising ticket volume of same type: automate that class.
toil.example: # example: automating certificate renewal removes recurring pager toil
toil.integration: 1) Categorize on-call work. 2) Prioritize top toil. 3) Automate. 4) Set toil budget goals.

incident triage.summary: Incident triage rapidly assesses impact, severity, and next diagnostic steps under time pressure.
incident triage.problem: It structures chaos into roles, communication, and mitigation.
incident triage.mechanics: Declare incident; assign IC; assess user impact; mitigate (rollback/scale); communicate; later investigate deeply.
incident triage.tradeoffs: Premature deep debugging delays mitigation. Blameless culture improves signal.
incident triage.troubleshoot: Floundering: lack of IC/roles. Use checklists.
incident triage.example: # severity rubric: SEV1 user-wide outage → page immediately
incident triage.integration: 1) Write severity definitions. 2) Train IC role. 3) Mitigation runbooks. 4) Postmortems.

postmortem.summary: A blameless postmortem documents what happened, impact, root causes, and corrective actions after an incident.
postmortem.problem: It turns outages into systemic learning.
postmortem.mechanics: Gather timeline/metrics; analyze contributing causes; assign owners/dates for fixes; share widely.
postmortem.tradeoffs: Without follow-up tracking, postmortems are theater.
postmortem.troubleshoot: Repeated incidents: actions not done or wrong causes.
postmortem.example: # template: summary, impact, timeline, root causes, actions
postmortem.integration: 1) Mandatory for SEV1/2. 2) Blameless facilitation. 3) Track actions to close. 4) Share learnings.

least privilege.summary: Least privilege grants only the permissions required for a task—nothing more.
least privilege.problem: It limits blast radius of breaches and mistakes.
least privilege.mechanics: Start from deny; add needed verbs/resources; prefer short-lived credentials; review periodically.
least privilege.tradeoffs: Over-tight permissions slow delivery—use break-glass with audit.
least privilege.troubleshoot: AccessDenied storms after tightening: iterate with logs.
least privilege.integration: 1) Replace * policies. 2) Role per service. 3) JIT elevation. 4) Quarterly access reviews.

secrets manager.summary: A secrets manager stores and rotates credentials centrally (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault) with audited access.
secrets manager.problem: It removes secrets from code, images, and developer laptops.
secrets manager.mechanics: App fetches secret at runtime with identity; manager rotates and versions; old versions invalidated.
secrets manager.tradeoffs: Env vars still leak—prefer runtime fetch + short cache. Pandemic of secret sprawl needs inventory.
secrets manager.troubleshoot: Fetch failures: IAM or network endpoint. Cache carefully.
secrets manager.integration: 1) Move secrets out of Git. 2) Grant identity-based access. 3) Enable rotation. 4) Audit usage.

SAST.summary: SAST (static application security testing) analyzes source/bytecode for vulnerabilities without running the app.
SAST.problem: It catches injection, secrets, and insecure patterns early in CI.
SAST.mechanics: Scanner parses code; reports findings; triage severities; fix or suppress with justification.
SAST.tradeoffs: Noise kills adoption—tune rules. DAST/SCA complement SAST.
SAST.troubleshoot: Missed vulns: unsupported frameworks. Keep analyzers updated.
SAST.integration: 1) Add SAST in CI. 2) Gate on high severity. 3) Triage weekly. 4) Train on common findings.

SBOM.summary: An SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) lists components/dependencies in an artifact for vulnerability and license tracking.
SBOM.problem: It answers “what’s in this image/binary?” during CVEs.
SBOM.mechanics: Generate SBOM at build; store beside artifact; scan against CVE DBs; alert on critical hits.
SBOM.tradeoffs: SBOM without process is unused data—wire to response playbooks.
SBOM.troubleshoot: Missing deps: generator config. Re-generate every build.
SBOM.integration: 1) Generate SBOM in CI. 2) Sign/store. 3) Scan continuously. 4) On CVE, query SBOMs.

container scanning.summary: Container scanning analyzes images for known CVEs in OS packages and app dependencies.
container scanning.problem: It reduces shipping critically vulnerable images.
container scanning.mechanics: Scan on build and periodically in registry; fail CI on severity thresholds; rebuild from patched bases.
container scanning.tradeoffs: Scanners have false positives; accept risk formally. Patching base images is highest leverage.
container scanning.troubleshoot: Same CVE after rebuild: pin moved or app deps. Check digests.
container scanning.integration: 1) Scan in CI. 2) Block criticals. 3) Automate base updates. 4) Rescan stored images.

image signing/provenance.summary: Image signing and provenance attest that an image was built by a trusted pipeline from known source (cosign/SLSA).
image signing/provenance.problem: It mitigates supply-chain tampering and untrusted tags.
image signing/provenance.mechanics: CI signs digest; cluster admission verifies signature/attestation before run.
image signing/provenance.tradeoffs: Key management is hard—keyless OIDC helps. Unsigned legacy images need migration.
image signing/provenance.troubleshoot: Admission rejects: missing signature or wrong identity—check CI settings.
image signing/provenance.integration: 1) Sign in CI. 2) Enforce verify in cluster. 3) Prefer digests. 4) Document trusted identities.

firewall.summary: A firewall filters packets/connections by policy (host iptables/nftables, cloud SG/NACL, network appliances).
firewall.problem: It reduces attack surface by allowing only needed paths.
firewall.mechanics: Define deny-by-default; open required ports between tiers; log drops for forensics.
firewall.tradeoffs: Over-complex rulesets become outage sources—keep simple tiers.
firewall.troubleshoot: Silent drops: check counters/logs. Change windows matter.
firewall.example:
sudo iptables -L -n | head
# prefer nftables/ufw/SG IaC in modern setups
firewall.integration: 1) Default deny. 2) Codify rules. 3) Log drops. 4) Review quarterly.

subnetting.summary: Subnetting divides IP space into networks for routing, isolation, and blast-radius control.
subnetting.problem: It structures VPCs and on-prem networks.
subnetting.mechanics: Allocate prefixes per tier/AZ; size for growth; document in IPAM. Avoid overlaps with partners.
subnetting.tradeoffs: Too-small subnets force painful renumbering; too-large waste space and widen broadcast domains (L2).
subnetting.troubleshoot: Overlap incidents: IPAM audit. Wrong mask: connectivity half-works.
subnetting.integration: 1) Create IPAM plan. 2) Standard subnet sizes. 3) Encode in Terraform. 4) Reserve spare capacity.

DNS.summary: DNS maps names to records (A/AAAA/CNAME) used by apps and users to locate services.
DNS.problem: Most distributed systems fail when DNS is wrong or cached stale.
DNS.mechanics: Clients query resolvers; answers cache for TTL; cutovers must respect caches. Split-horizon serves different answers internally.
DNS.tradeoffs: Service discovery may supplement DNS (k8s, Consul). Low TTL vs query load trade-off.
DNS.troubleshoot: Stale answers: TTL. SERVFAIL: upstream. Use dig +trace.
DNS.example:
dig +short api.internal A
dig SOA example.com
DNS.integration: 1) Manage zones as code. 2) Plan TTL for changes. 3) Monitor resolution errors. 4) Document private zones.

DNS outage.summary: A DNS outage is when resolution fails or returns wrong data, breaking service discovery even if backends are healthy.
DNS outage.problem: It presents as widespread timeouts with healthy hosts.
DNS outage.mechanics: Triage: dig from multiple resolvers; check authoritative; roll back zone changes; lower blast via cached IPs only temporarily.
DNS outage.tradeoffs: Hardcoding IPs is a brittle mitigation. Multi-resolver and health-checked failover help.
DNS outage.troubleshoot: App errors without backend CPU: suspect DNS. Check /etc/resolv.conf and ndots in k8s.
DNS outage.integration: 1) Redundant DNS. 2) Change control for zones. 3) Runbooks for rollback. 4) Synthetic DNS checks.

TLS certificate.summary: A TLS certificate binds a public key to identities (DNS names) and is trusted via a CA chain.
TLS certificate.problem: It enables authenticated encryption for HTTPS and mTLS.
TLS certificate.mechanics: Issue cert; install on LB/server; clients validate chain+hostname+expiry. Automate renewal (ACME).
TLS certificate.tradeoffs: Long-lived certs increase risk; short-lived need reliable automation.
TLS certificate.troubleshoot: Browser errors: name mismatch, incomplete chain, expired. openssl s_client debugs.
TLS certificate.example: echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates -ext subjectAltName
TLS certificate.integration: 1) Automate issuance/renewal. 2) Alert on expiry. 3) Serve full chain. 4) Use SAN for all names.

TCP.summary: TCP provides reliable ordered byte streams—used by most admin protocols and HTTP.
TCP.problem: Understanding TCP helps debug timeouts, resets, and performance.
TCP.mechanics: Connect via handshake; transfer with acks; close with FIN/RST. Firewalls must allow SYN paths.
TCP.tradeoffs: UDP for latency-sensitive/loss-tolerant. TLS wraps TCP commonly.
TCP.troubleshoot: Resets: SG/RST from app. Use ss/tcpdump carefully.
TCP.integration: 1) Set timeouts. 2) Monitor retransmits. 3) Keepalive thoughtfully. 4) Document required ports.

virtual machine.summary: A VM virtualizes hardware so a full guest OS runs isolated on a hypervisor.
virtual machine.problem: Cloud instances are VMs with API lifecycle.
virtual machine.mechanics: Boot from image; attach disks/NICs; patch guest. Stronger isolation than containers sharing a kernel.
virtual machine.tradeoffs: Heavier than containers; slower density. Use for different kernels/strong tenancy.
virtual machine.example: # cloud: launch instance from hardened image
virtual machine.integration: 1) Golden images. 2) Autopatch. 3) Prefer containers for apps when suitable. 4) Monitor host contention.

upstream/load balancing.summary: In reverse proxies (nginx), upstreams define backend server pools and load-balancing policy.
upstream/load balancing.problem: They distribute requests and remove unhealthy backends.
upstream/load balancing.mechanics: Proxy passes to upstream servers; weights and health determine selection. Timeouts prevent wedged backends hanging workers.
upstream/load balancing.tradeoffs: Service meshes move some of this into sidecars. Keep timeouts aligned end-to-end.
upstream/load balancing.troubleshoot: 502/504: all upstreams down or timeouts—check upstream health.
upstream/load balancing.integration: 1) Define upstream pools. 2) Configure health checks. 3) Align timeouts. 4) Observe error rates.

reverse proxy.summary: A reverse proxy terminates client connections and forwards to internal backends (nginx, Envoy, ALB).
reverse proxy.problem: It centralizes TLS, routing, compression, and security controls.
reverse proxy.mechanics: Client→proxy→backend. Proxy adds X-Forwarded-* carefully; backends trust only known proxies.
reverse proxy.tradeoffs: Extra hop adds latency but simplifies certs and policy. Misconfigured buffering hurts streaming.
reverse proxy.troubleshoot: Bad gateways: upstream down. Redirect loops: scheme/headers wrong.
reverse proxy.integration: 1) Terminate TLS at proxy. 2) Standardize forwarded headers. 3) Health-check backends. 4) Rate-limit edges.

DO-B-0046.summary: /etc holds config, /var variable data/logs, /home user dirs, /tmp ephemeral files, /proc process/kernel APIs.
DO-B-0046.integration: 1) Follow FHS in packaging. 2) Monitor /var disk. 3) Don’t store durable state only in /tmp. 4) Document mounts.
DO-B-0046.shortAnswer: /etc holds config, /var variable data/logs, /home user dirs, /tmp ephemeral files, /proc process/kernel APIs.
DO-B-0046.answer: Use the FHS mental model while debugging hosts and containers: configs under /etc, state/logs under /var, runtime introspection in /proc.

DO-B-0047.summary: Linux permissions use owner/group/other rwx bits plus ownership; directories need execute to traverse.
DO-B-0047.integration: 1) Non-root services. 2) Tighten modes. 3) Align container UIDs. 4) Audit world-writable paths.
DO-B-0047.shortAnswer: Linux permissions use owner/group/other rwx bits plus ownership; directories need execute to traverse.
DO-B-0047.answer: chmod/chown change mode/owner; umask sets defaults. Services should run as non-root with tight modes on secrets.

DO-B-0048.summary: Use ss/lsof to map ports to PIDs, then inspect that process.
DO-B-0048.integration: 1) Standardize on ss. 2) Document required ports. 3) Restrict via SG/firewall. 4) Alert on unexpected listeners.
DO-B-0048.shortAnswer: Use ss/lsof to map ports to PIDs, then inspect that process.
DO-B-0048.answer: ss -ltnp shows listening TCP sockets with processes; cross-check with lsof -i. In containers, check from the correct network namespace.

DO-B-0049.summary: Regions are geographic AWS areas; Availability Zones are isolated data centers within a region.
DO-B-0049.integration: 1) Multi-AZ for prod. 2) Pin region in IaC. 3) Document DR region. 4) Test failover.
DO-B-0049.shortAnswer: Regions are geographic AWS areas; Availability Zones are isolated data centers within a region.
DO-B-0049.answer: Deploy across AZs for HA; pick regions for latency and compliance. Cross-region is for DR, not default HA.

DO-B-0050.summary: DNS names resources; TCP/UDP transport; HTTP is an application protocol; HTTPS is HTTP over TLS.
DO-B-0050.integration: 1) Diagram your request path. 2) Monitor DNS and TLS separately. 3) Prefer HTTPS everywhere. 4) Document ports.
DO-B-0050.shortAnswer: DNS names resources; TCP/UDP transport; HTTP is an application protocol; HTTPS is HTTP over TLS.
DO-B-0050.answer: Most web apps use DNS → TCP → TLS → HTTP. UDP is common for DNS queries and real-time media.

DO-B-0051.answer: Together they cover compute, storage, access, networking, databases, and observability on AWS.

DO-B-0052.answer: Events trigger workflows; jobs can be parallel/dependent; pin action versions and least-privilege permissions.
